title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: On that bright evening of August 25, Prince Andrew lay propped on his elbow in a broken-down shed in the village of Knyazkovo at the far end of his regiment's camp. Through a gap in the broken wall he could see, beside the wooden fence, a row of thirty-year-old birches with their lower branches trimmed off, a field with sheaves of oats standing in it, and some bushes near which rose the smoke of campfires—the soldiers' kitchens.
Narrow and burdensome and useless to anyone as his life now seemed to him, Prince Andrew on the eve of battle felt as agitated and irritable as he had seven years before at Austerlitz.

He had received and given the orders for the next day's battle and had nothing more to do. But his thoughts—the simplest, clearest, and therefore most terrible thoughts—would give him no peace. He knew that tomorrow's battle would be the most terrible he had ever been in, and for the first time in his life, the possibility of death presented itself not in relation to any worldly matter or its effect on others, but simply in relation to himself, to his own soul—vividly, plainly, terribly, and almost as a certainty. And from the height of this awareness, all that had previously tormented and preoccupied him was suddenly illuminated by a cold white light without shadows, without perspective, without distinction. All of life appeared to him like magic-lantern pictures he had long been gazing at through a glass by artificial light. Now he suddenly saw those badly painted images in the clear daylight, without the glass. "Yes, yes! There they are, those false images that excited, enchanted, and tormented me," he said to himself, reviewing the principal pictures of the magic lantern of life and seeing them now in the cold white light of his clear perception of death. "There they are, those crudely painted figures that once seemed splendid and mysterious. Glory, the good of society, love of a woman, the Fatherland itself—how important these pictures seemed, with what profound meaning they appeared to be filled! And it is all so simple, pale, and crude in the cold white light of this morning I feel dawning for me." The three great sorrows of his life held his attention in particular: his love for a woman, his father's death, and the French invasion that had overrun half of Russia. "Love... that little girl who seemed to me overflowing with mysterious power! Yes, I loved her. I made romantic plans of love and happiness with her! Oh, what a fool I was!" he said aloud bitterly. "I believed in some ideal love that was to keep her faithful for the whole year of my absence! Like the gentle dove in the fable, she was to pine apart from me... But it was much simpler than that... It was all very simple and horrible."

"When my father built Bald Hills, he thought the place was his: his land, his air, his peasants. But Napoleon came and swept him aside, unconscious of his existence, as he might brush a chip from his path, and his Bald Hills and his whole life fell to pieces. Princess Mary says it is a trial sent from above. What is the trial for, when he is gone and will never return? He is gone! For whom then is the trial intended? The Fatherland, the destruction of Moscow! And tomorrow I shall be killed—perhaps not even by a Frenchman but by one of our own men, by a soldier firing a musket close to my ear, as one of them did yesterday—and the French will come and take me by the head and feet and fling me into a ditch so I won't stink under their noses, and new conditions of life will arise that will seem perfectly ordinary to others but about which I shall know nothing. I shall not exist..."

He looked at the row of birches shining in the sunshine, with their motionless green and yellow foliage and white bark. "To die... to be killed tomorrow... That I should not exist... That all this should still be, but not me..."

And the birches with their light and shade, the curly clouds, the smoke of the campfires, and everything around him changed and seemed terrible and menacing. A cold shiver ran down his spine. He rose quickly, went out of the shed, and began pacing.
When he returned, voices were heard outside the shed. "Who's that?" he called.

The red-nosed Captain Timokhin, formerly Dolokhov's company commander but now, due to the shortage of officers, a battalion commander, shyly entered the shed followed by an adjutant and the regimental paymaster.
Prince Andrew rose quickly, listened to the business they had come about, gave them additional instructions, and was about to dismiss them when he heard a familiar, lisping voice behind the shed.
"Devil take it!" said the voice of a man stumbling over something.

Prince Andrew looked out of the shed and saw Pierre, who had tripped over a pole on the ground and nearly fallen, coming his way. It was unpleasant to Prince Andrew to meet people from his own circle in general, and Pierre especially, for Pierre reminded him of all the painful moments of his last visit to Moscow.
"You? What a surprise!" he said. "What brings you here? This is unexpected!"

As he said this, his eyes and face expressed more than coldness—they expressed hostility, which Pierre noticed at once. He had approached the shed full of animation, but seeing Prince Andrew's face, he felt constrained and uncomfortable.
"I've come... simply... you know... come... it interests me," said Pierre, who had so often that day senselessly repeated the word "interesting." "I wanted to see the battle."

"Oh yes, and what do the Masonic brothers say about war? How would they stop it?" said Prince Andrew sarcastically. "Well, and how's Moscow? And my family? Have they reached Moscow at last?" he asked more seriously.
"Yes, they have. Julie Drubetskaya told me. I went to see them but missed them. They've gone to your estate near Moscow."
